title: MCP 2026-07-28: Stateless Protocol, MCP Apps & Tasks
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol steering group published a release candidate for the next protocol revision, dated **2026-07-28** (the RC was published in early-to-mid July 2026; the final spec is scheduled to ship on that date). It's the biggest change to MCP's wire protocol since the original 2024 release, and the headline shift is that MCP moves from a stateful, session-oriented protocol to a **stateless** one.

This page tracks what changes and why it matters for anyone running or building MCP servers (like the ones Claude Code connects to via `mcp__<server>__*` tools).

---

## MCP Goes Stateless

Previous MCP revisions required an `initialize` handshake that established a protocol-level session between client and server, which then had to be kept alive (or reconnected with matching state) for the duration of the interaction. The 2026-07-28 revision removes both the handshake and the protocol-level session entirely.

**Why it matters operationally:** servers can now be scaled behind a plain round-robin load balancer. There's no more need for sticky sessions or a shared session store (e.g., Redis) to keep multiple server replicas in sync — any replica can answer any request, because no server-side session state is assumed between calls.

This is a significant simplification for anyone self-hosting MCP servers at scale, and removes a whole class of "server restarted and dropped my session" bugs.

---

## MCP Apps

**MCP Apps** let a server ship an interactive HTML interface alongside its tools, which the host application renders inside a **sandboxed iframe** rather than as plain text or JSON.

- Tools declare their UI templates ahead of time (not generated on the fly), so hosts can prefetch, cache, and security-review the UI before any tool actually runs.
- The rendered UI talks back to the host over the *same* JSON-RPC base protocol used for everything else in MCP — so a button click inside an MCP App's iframe goes through the same audit and consent path as a direct tool call. There's no separate, less-audited side channel for UI-triggered actions.

This targets a real gap in the original spec: MCP servers that wanted rich output (dashboards, forms, visualizations) previously had to either return raw HTML strings with no sandboxing story, or fall back to plain text/markdown.

---

## Tasks Extension

The **Tasks extension** reworks how long-running tool calls behave under the new stateless model. Instead of a client holding a connection open while a slow tool executes, a server can respond to `tools/call` with a **task handle**, and the client then drives progress with:

- `tasks/get` — poll for status/result
- `tasks/update` — (server → client) push a progress update
- `tasks/cancel` — cancel an in-flight task

Task creation is **server-directed**: the client advertises that it supports the Tasks extension, but the server decides whether a given call is worth running as a background task versus answering synchronously. This fits naturally with the stateless transport — a task can be picked up by a different server replica than the one that started it, since progress is tracked via the task handle rather than an open connection.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization** extension — previously experimental — was promoted to **stable** status in this cycle. It gives organizations a centralized way to control which MCP servers their users can connect to and what those servers can access, enforced through the org's existing identity provider (SSO/OIDC) rather than per-server credential management.

For teams running many MCP servers internally (as opposed to a handful of personal ones), this closes a gap where access control had been left entirely to each server's own auth implementation.

---

## What This Means for Claude Code Users

Claude Code's `mcp__<server>__*` tool integration sits on top of this protocol, so most of the stateless/Tasks changes are invisible to end users — they show up as more reliable reconnects and better support for long-running tool calls (e.g., a search or crawl that used to time out a stateful connection). MCP Apps is the more visible change: expect MCP servers to start shipping richer, interactive tool output instead of walls of JSON or markdown over the coming months as hosts add rendering support.

The 2026 roadmap for MCP (published alongside the RC) lists transport scalability, agent-to-agent communication, governance maturation, and enterprise readiness as its four priorities — the stateless protocol and EMA promotion both fall directly out of the "scalability" and "enterprise readiness" pillars.
